name: Integrated Pest Management and Organic Pest Control
objectives: For one crop on your own farm, list prevention steps that keep pests from building up before the season starts, naming at least three steps that fit your crop

Walking your own field once a week, scout a set number of plants and identify fall armyworm, Tuta absoluta and common natural enemies from their signs, checking at least 50 plants (or 20 tomato plants) and recording what you find

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The four IPM steps, starting with prevention
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the prevention steps that keep pests from building up on one of your crops.
This lesson builds toward: For one crop on your own farm, you will list prevention steps that keep pests from building up before the season starts, naming at least three steps that fit your crop.
FAO describes integrated pest management (IPM) as looking at all the ways to control pests, combining the right ones, and using pesticides only when they are justified. It works in four steps: prevent, monitor, decide and act. Most of the savings come from the first step.
Prevention means making the field a bad home for pests and a good home for the crop. Plant certified seed of a variety suited to your area, and resistant or tolerant varieties where they exist. Rotate crops so pests that live in the soil or on residues lose their food: for example, maize, then beans, then sorghum. Plant on time and all at once with your neighbours, so pests do not move from late fields to early ones. Feed the soil, because weak plants are attacked first.
Keep the field clean: remove and destroy plants with virus or disease, take out volunteer plants and weeds that host pests, and clean tools and boots. In tomatoes, raise seedlings in a clean, netted nursery so they go to the field free of Tuta absoluta and whiteflies. Leave flowering borders and hedges, because they feed the insects that eat pests.
A farmer in Ghana who rotates maize with groundnuts, plants early with her neighbours and pulls sick plants each week often sprays far less than one who plants maize on the same plot every season.
Step by step:
- Write down the main pests and diseases of your crop (ask extension or a plant clinic).
- Choose certified seed of a suitable, resistant or tolerant variety.
- Plan a rotation and plant on time, at the same time as your neighbours.
- Plan field hygiene: remove sick plants, volunteers and host weeds; clean tools.
- Leave flowering borders for natural enemies.
Words to know:
- IPM: integrated pest management: preventing pests, watching for them, deciding when action pays, and combining many controls, with pesticides only when justified.
- Prevention: steps taken before pests arrive so they cannot build up.
- Rotation: growing a different crop on the same plot each season.
- Volunteer plant: a crop plant that grows by itself from last season's seed and can carry pests.
Official sources:
- FAO: Integrated Pest Management
Try it now: Pick one crop you will grow next season. Write its three worst pests or diseases, then write at least three prevention steps you will take before planting (seed, rotation, timing, hygiene, borders).
You can now name the four IPM steps and list prevention steps that keep pests from building up on your crop.

check.q: Which IPM step usually saves a farmer the most money?
options: Spraying every week
Buying a stronger product
Prevention before pests arrive
Spraying the neighbour's field
check.why: Prevention stops pests building up, so fewer controls are needed later.

check.q: Your maize had heavy pest damage on the same plot three seasons running. What prevention step fits best?
options: Rotate the plot to beans or groundnuts next season
Plant maize later than your neighbours
Leave last season's maize stalks standing
Plant uncertified seed saved from damaged cobs
check.why: Rotation breaks the pest's cycle by taking away its food plant.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Scouting and identifying fall armyworm and Tuta absoluta
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Scout a field on a set path and identify fall armyworm, Tuta absoluta and natural enemies from their signs.
This lesson builds toward: Walking your own field once a week, you will scout a set number of plants and identify fall armyworm, Tuta absoluta and common natural enemies from their signs, checking at least 50 plants (or 20 tomato plants) and recording what you find.
Scouting means walking your field on a schedule and checking a set number of plants, so you see trouble early and can count it. Scout at least once a week, more often for young maize and for tomatoes. Walk a W or zigzag path so you check the whole field, not only the edges. In maize, stop at five places and check 10 plants in a row at each, 50 plants in total. In a small tomato plot, check 20 plants spread across the beds.
Fall armyworm arrived in Africa in 2016 and is now found in most of the continent. On young maize, look for small "window panes" (thin, see-through patches) on the leaves, then ragged holes and wet, sawdust-like droppings in the funnel (whorl). The caterpillar has a pale upside-down Y on its head and four dark spots in a square near its tail. Egg masses sit on leaves under a layer of fuzzy scales. A plant counts as infested if it has fresh damage or a live caterpillar.
Tuta absoluta, the tomato leafminer, came from South America and spread across Africa within a few years; icipe reports that in northern Nigeria in 2016 it destroyed most of the tomato crop. Its tiny caterpillars tunnel inside leaves, making pale, see-through blotches (mines) with dark droppings, and bore small holes into stems and fruit. The adult is a small grey-brown moth that hides in the day.
Also look for friends: ladybirds and their larvae, lacewings, spiders, earwigs, ants and small parasitic wasps, and caterpillars that look sick, soft or covered in fungus. FAO notes that natural enemies already kill many fall armyworm caterpillars in African fields. If you are not sure what you see, take a clear photo and ask an extension officer or plant clinic; in some countries FAO's FAMEWS app records fall armyworm sightings.
Step by step:
- Choose a scouting day each week and carry a notebook or phone.
- Walk a W path; stop at 5 places in maize (10 plants each) or 20 tomato plants spread out.
- On each plant, check leaves, the funnel or growing tip, stems and fruit.
- Count plants with fresh damage or live pests; note egg masses.
- Note natural enemies you see.
- Photograph anything you cannot identify and ask extension or a plant clinic.
Words to know:
- Scouting: walking a field on a schedule and checking a set number of plants for pests, diseases and natural enemies.
- Funnel (whorl): the rolled-up young leaves at the top of a young maize plant.
- Leaf mine: a pale tunnel or blotch inside a leaf made by a tiny caterpillar feeding between the leaf surfaces.
- Natural enemy: an insect, spider, fungus or other living thing that kills pests.
Official sources:
- CIMMYT, USAID and partners: Fall Armyworm in Africa: A Guide for Integrated Pest Management (2018)
- icipe: Insect of the Month: Tomato leafminer, Tuta absoluta
- FAO: mobile application to support the fight against Fall Armyworm in Africa (FAMEWS)
Try it now: Scout one of your fields today on a W path: 50 maize plants or 20 tomato plants. Write how many plants had fresh damage or live pests, any egg masses, and every natural enemy you saw.
You can now scout a field on a set path, identify fall armyworm and Tuta absoluta from their signs, and spot natural enemies.

check.q: You see wet, sawdust-like droppings and ragged holes in the funnel of young maize. What is the most likely pest?
options: Tomato leafminer
Aphids
Fall armyworm
Termites
check.why: Ragged holes and wet droppings in the funnel are classic fall armyworm signs.

check.q: Why walk a W path when scouting instead of checking the plants near the gate?
options: It is faster
Pests only live in the middle
It uses less water
It checks the whole field, not just the edges
check.why: A W path samples every part of the field, so the count reflects the real level.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Thresholds and records: deciding when to act
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare your scouting count with an action threshold and record whether to act or keep watching.
This lesson builds toward: Given your scouting counts and a threshold from extension, you will decide whether to act now or keep watching, and record the decision, matching the threshold rule every time.
Seeing a pest does not mean you must spray. An action threshold is the level of pest or damage at which control is worth its cost. Below it, natural enemies and the crop can usually cope, and spraying would waste money and kill your helpers. Get the threshold for each main pest, crop stage and area from your extension officer or research institute (such as KALRO in Kenya), because it changes with crop stage, price and local research.
Turn your count into a percentage: plants with fresh damage or live pests, divided by plants checked, times 100. Example: you checked 50 maize plants and 9 had fresh fall armyworm damage, so 9 / 50 x 100 = 18%. If extension told you to act at 20% at this stage, you keep watching and scout again in a few days. If next week it is 26%, you act. Young maize can usually stand less damage than older maize, so thresholds are often different by stage.
Write every visit down. A simple record has the date, field, crop stage, plants checked, plants infested, the percentage, natural enemies seen, the threshold, your decision and what you did. After a few seasons your records show when pests arrive on your farm, which controls worked and what they cost. A paper notebook works; so does a phone spreadsheet or a farm app.
Step by step:
- Ask extension for the threshold for each main pest and crop stage.
- After scouting, count plants checked and plants infested.
- Work out the percentage: infested / checked x 100.
- Compare with the threshold: below = keep watching; at or above = act.
- Write the date, numbers, natural enemies, decision and action in your record.
Words to know:
- Action threshold: the level of pest or damage at which control is worth the cost.
- Infested: having pests or fresh damage from pests.
- Crop stage: how far the crop has grown, for example seedling, knee-high, tasselling, flowering, fruiting.
Official sources:
- FAO: Integrated Pest Management
- CIMMYT, USAID and partners: Fall Armyworm in Africa: A Guide for Integrated Pest Management (2018)
Try it now: Use the count from your scouting in the last lesson. Work out the percentage of infested plants, ask your extension officer for the threshold at your crop stage, and fill in your first record line with your decision.
You can now turn a scouting count into a percentage, compare it with a threshold, and record your decision.

check.q: You checked 50 plants and 15 had fresh damage. What is the infestation?
Your count is 12% and the extension threshold for this stage is 20%. What do you do?
options: Spray today to be safe
Pull up the crop
Double the spray rate
Keep watching, scout again soon and record it
check.why: Below the threshold, control does not pay yet; you keep scouting and recording.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Controlling pests with less poison

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Push-pull and natural enemies
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a push-pull plot and protect the natural enemies on your farm.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pest problem on your crop, you will choose and set up non-chemical controls such as push-pull, natural enemies, traps and biological products, before any synthetic pesticide is used.
Push-pull was developed by icipe, with partners, for maize and sorghum in East Africa. You plant desmodium between the rows of maize. Desmodium gives off smells that push stemborer moths away from the crop. Around the plot you plant a border of a fodder grass (brachiaria in the climate-smart version for drier areas, napier grass in the original), which pulls the moths to it and traps them. Desmodium also suppresses striga weed and adds nitrogen to the soil, and both plants are good cattle feed.
icipe studies in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania found far less fall armyworm damage in climate-smart push-pull fields than in maize grown alone, and higher grain yields. Push-pull takes work to set up and you need desmodium seed or vines and grass splits, so start with a small plot, ask extension or an icipe-trained farmer for the layout, and follow icipe's farmer guide.
Natural enemies are free workers. Ants, earwigs, spiders, ladybirds and lacewings eat eggs and young caterpillars; small wasps lay their eggs inside pests; fungi and viruses kill caterpillars. FAO notes that these already kill a large share of fall armyworm in African fields. icipe has released a tiny wasp from South America that attacks only Tuta absoluta in Kenya. To protect them: spray only when the threshold says so, choose selective products, keep flowering plants and hedges around fields, and leave some ground cover.
Step by step:
- Mark out a small push-pull plot (ask extension or icipe's guide for the layout).
- Plant the border grass (brachiaria or napier) around the plot first.
- Plant desmodium between the maize or sorghum rows.
- Cut the grass and desmodium for livestock feed, leaving the plants to regrow.
- Protect natural enemies: no needless spraying, keep flowers and ground cover.
Words to know:
- Push-pull: an icipe system where an intercrop (desmodium) pushes pests away and a border grass pulls them out of the crop.
- Desmodium: a low-growing legume planted between cereal rows; it repels stemborer moths, suppresses striga and adds nitrogen.
- Striga: a parasitic weed with pink or purple flowers that attaches to maize and sorghum roots and steals their food.
- Parasitic wasp: a tiny wasp that lays its eggs in or on a pest, and its young kill the pest.
Official sources:
- icipe: Push-pull technology halts fall armyworm
- icipe: New study unravels how push-pull conquers fall armyworm (how desmodium and brachiaria work)
- icipe: Climate-Smart Push-Pull farmer guide (revised edition)
- icipe: Insect of the Month: Tomato leafminer, Tuta absoluta
Try it now: Draw a sketch of a small push-pull plot for your maize or sorghum, with the border grass, the desmodium rows and the crop rows. Then write two things you will change on your farm to protect natural enemies.
You can now explain how push-pull works, sketch a push-pull plot, and name ways to protect natural enemies.

check.q: In push-pull, what does the desmodium between the maize rows do?
options: Pulls pests into the maize
Pushes stemborer moths away and suppresses striga
Shades the maize so it grows taller
Kills ladybirds
check.why: Desmodium's smell repels moths and it suppresses striga; the border grass does the pulling.

check.q: Which habit protects natural enemies best?
options: Spraying a broad pesticide every week
Clearing every flower and hedge around the field
Burning crop residues and all ground cover
Spraying only above the threshold and keeping flowering borders
check.why: Fewer sprays and flowering plants keep natural enemies alive and fed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Traps, botanical and biological options
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose and set up traps and approved botanical or biological controls for a pest problem.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pest problem on your crop, you will choose and set up non-chemical controls such as push-pull, natural enemies, traps and biological products, before any synthetic pesticide is used.
Traps help you watch and lower pest numbers. Pheromone traps use the smell of a female moth to catch males: icipe uses mass trapping as part of its IPM for Tuta absoluta, and pheromone traps for fall armyworm tell you when moths arrive so you scout harder. Yellow sticky cards catch whiteflies, aphids and leafminer adults; blue ones catch thrips. Replace lures and cards as the supplier says, and count catches each week in your record.
Hand-picking works on small plots: crush fall armyworm egg masses and young caterpillars, and pick off and destroy Tuta-mined leaves and damaged fruit (bury them deep or seal them in a bag in the sun, never leave them on the ground).
Biological products use living things or their natural products against pests: for example products based on the bacterium Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis), on fungi that infect insects, or on insect viruses. icipe develops fungus-based biopesticides. They are usually gentle on natural enemies, but they act slowly, need to hit young caterpillars, and must be stored as the label says. In many countries they must be registered like any pesticide, so check the regulator's list.
Botanical options come from plants, such as neem. Registered neem products have a label you can follow. Home-made extracts are widely used, but their strength varies and they can still harm natural enemies, skin and eyes, so ask your extension officer how they are used in your area, wear gloves, and test on a few plants first.
Step by step:
- Match the tool to the pest: pheromone traps for moths, yellow cards for whiteflies and aphids, blue for thrips.
- Hang traps at crop height and count catches weekly.
- Hand-pick and destroy egg masses, young caterpillars and mined leaves.
- If more is needed, choose a registered biological or botanical product.
- Apply it to young caterpillars, as its label says, and record it.
Words to know:
- Pheromone trap: a trap baited with an insect's mating smell; it catches males and shows when pests arrive.
- Biopesticide: a pest control product made from living things such as bacteria, fungi or viruses, or their natural products.
- Bt: Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium used in biopesticides; it kills some caterpillars when they eat it.
- Botanical: a pest control product made from plants, such as neem.
Official sources:
- icipe: Insect of the Month: Tomato leafminer, Tuta absoluta
- CIMMYT, USAID and partners: Fall Armyworm in Africa: A Guide for Integrated Pest Management (2018)
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya)
- National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC, Nigeria)
Try it now: For the worst pest on your crop, write which trap you would use and where you would hang it, what you would hand-pick, and one biological or botanical option. Then check whether that product is on your country's registered list or ask your agro-dealer to show you its registration.
You can now choose traps, hand-picking and approved biological or botanical controls for a pest and set them up.

check.q: You grow tomatoes and want to know when Tuta absoluta moths arrive. What do you set up?
options: A pheromone trap for Tuta absoluta
A blue sticky card
A bucket of water in the store
A scarecrow
check.why: A pheromone trap baited for Tuta catches the male moths and shows when they arrive.

check.q: A Bt-based biopesticide works best when you:
options: Spray it on big, old caterpillars at noon
Mix it with any other chemical
Apply it to young caterpillars as its label says
Store it in the sun
check.why: Biological products act slowly and work best on young caterpillars, used as the label says.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Pesticides as the last step, and slowing resistance
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a pesticide's registration, follow its label with protective equipment, and plan group rotation to slow resistance.
This lesson builds toward: When a pesticide is truly needed, you will check that the product is registered, follow its label and wear the protective equipment it lists, with no step skipped. Across a season of spraying decisions, you will rotate pesticide groups and keep a spray record to slow resistance, never using the same group on the same pest generation twice in a row.
Use a synthetic pesticide only when your count is above the threshold and other controls are not enough. First check that the product is registered for your crop and pest in your country: the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria, the Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) in Ghana, and the Sahelian Pesticides Committee (CSP) for CILSS countries such as Senegal and Burkina Faso. Each keeps a list of registered products; check it, and buy only sealed, labelled containers from a licensed agro-dealer. Fake and unregistered products are common.
The label is the law. Read it all before you open the container: the crops and pests it is for, the rate, how to mix, when to spray, the protective equipment, how long to wait before harvest (the pre-harvest interval) and before people go back into the field, and first aid. Wear what the label lists, usually gloves, boots, long sleeves and trousers, eye protection and a mask or respirator. Spray in calm, cool hours, never towards people, animals or water. Do not eat, drink or smoke while spraying, wash afterwards, and lock products away from children and food. Never put pesticide in a drink or food bottle.
Pests become resistant when the same kind of chemical is used again and again: the few that survive breed. Fall armyworm and Tuta absoluta are both known for this. Labels often show a group number or the active ingredient. Rotate between groups, do not use the same group on the same pest generation twice in a row, never under-dose or mix products yourself, and keep a spray record with the date, product, group, rate, field and pre-harvest date. In Kenya, a tomato grower who sprays the same product every few days often sees it stop working; one who scouts, traps and rotates groups keeps her few sprays working.
Step by step:
- Confirm the count is above the threshold and other controls are not enough.
- Check the product is registered for your crop and pest (PCPB, NAFDAC, EPA Ghana, CSP).
- Buy a sealed, labelled container from a licensed agro-dealer.
- Read the whole label; put on all the protective equipment it lists.
- Spray in calm, cool hours at the label rate; wash and store safely.
- Record the product, group, rate and the pre-harvest date; rotate groups next time.
Words to know:
- Registered pesticide: a product the national regulator has approved for named crops and pests.
- Label: the instructions on the container; following it is the law.
- PPE: personal protective equipment: gloves, boots, long clothes, eye protection and a mask or respirator.
- Pre-harvest interval: the time you must wait after spraying before you harvest; it is printed on the label.
- Resistance: when a pest no longer dies from a product that used to kill it.
- Mode-of-action group: a number or name that shows how a pesticide kills; rotate between groups to slow resistance.
Official sources:
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya)
- National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC, Nigeria)
- Environmental Protection Authority (Ghana)
- CILSS / INSAH: Sahelian Pesticides Committee (CSP) registration guide
- FAO: Integrated Pest Management
Try it now: Final task: write your one-season IPM plan for one crop on your farm: main pests, at least three prevention steps, your weekly scouting routine and record sheet, the thresholds you got from extension, the non-chemical controls you will use first, and a last-step pesticide plan (a product checked on your regulator's list, the label rules, your PPE, and how you will rotate groups).
You can now check that a pesticide is registered, follow its label with the right protective equipment, and rotate groups and keep records to slow resistance.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Prevention No prevention steps, or only "spray early". At least three prevention steps that fit the crop (seed, rotation, timing, hygiene or borders). Prevention steps are timed on a calendar and agreed with neighbours, such as planting together. Scouting routine Scouting is "when I see damage", with no plant count. A weekly day, a W path, a set number of plants and a record sheet with columns for pests and natural enemies. Includes photos of the main pests and natural enemies to identify them, and the record has been used for at least two weeks. Thresholds and decisions No thresholds; action is by habit. A threshold from extension for each main pest, with the percentage method written out. Thresholds are listed by crop stage, and a worked example from the learner's own counts is included. Non-chemical controls first Pesticide is the first and only control. At least two non-chemical controls (push-pull, traps, hand-picking, natural enemies, biological or botanical) are planned before any pesticide. Non-chemical controls are already set up, such as traps hanging or a push-pull plot planted. Safe, legal last step The product is not checked or the plan skips the label or PPE. The product is checked on the national regulator's list, and the plan follows the label, lists PPE and names the pre-harvest interval from the label. Also includes safe storage, disposal of empty containers as the label says, and first aid steps. Resistance and records One product used all season, no spray record. A spray record and a rotation between at least two groups. Rotation is planned by pest generation, and records include the cost of each control. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again with your extension officer.

check.q: An agro-dealer offers you an unlabelled bottle of insecticide at a low price. What do you do?
options: Buy it; it is cheaper
Mix it with water and test it
Refuse it and buy a sealed, labelled, registered product
Use half the bottle
check.why: Without a label you cannot know what it is, how to use it safely, or if it is registered.

check.q: You sprayed a product from group A last time. The pest is still above the threshold. What is best?
options: Spray group A again at double the rate
Spray a registered product from a different group
Mix group A with another product yourself
Spray group A every day
check.why: Rotating to a different group slows resistance; double rates and home mixes are unsafe and illegal.
